items.text: When painters turn to the essentially musical notion of rhythm in order to define what they consider one of the necessary elements of their own art, it is a sure sign that this art itself is trying to overstep its natural limits. <break time="0.8s" /> Nor are painters themselves unaware of the fact. <break time="0.8s" /> The arts of space, from architecture to sculpture and painting, have always included among their fundamental notions that of composition. <break time="0.8s" /> To compose is to arrange the parts of a picture in such a way that the proportions between their respective sizes, shapes, colors, and degrees of luminosity are pleasing to perceive. <break time="0.8s" /> The reason modern painters, especially since the time of Picasso, Braque, and Juan Gris, have added the notion of rhythm to that of composition is not mysterious. <break time="0.8s" /> For, indeed, rhythm implies composition, but it adds to it a regularly reoccurring pattern in the duration of sounds. <break time="0.8s" /> This is to say that, as soon as pictorial composition in space assumes the form of patterns of lines and colors successively perceived in time, composition becomes for us a rhythm.
